Analysis period classification: Period bins use right-closed intervals: (1999, 2016], (2016, 2017], (2017, 2019], (2019, 2021], (2021, 2025]. Year 2017 is assigned its own period rather than grouped with the initial recovery because annual data mixes pre- and post-hurricane months.
Why mean for employment: FRED employment is a stock measure (workers employed in a given pay period), not a flow. Summing monthly employment values would produce a nonsensical total. The annual average represents the typical employment level during the year.
Why sum for NPS: Recreation visits are a flow (events that occur during a period). Summing monthly visits produces the annual total. The NPS annual-file values match the sum of monthly values exactly for all available years in this dataset.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Recovery index construction
The recovery index is constructed as follows:
\[\text{Index}_{s,t} = \frac{x_{s,t}}{x_{s,2016}} \times 100\]
where \(x_{s,t}\) is the value of series \(s\) in year \(t\) and \(x_{s,2016}\) is the 2016 base-year value.
Series with no 2016 observation are excluded from indexed comparisons.
A&F real value added uses BEA Table 2.3 (chained 2012 dollars). This series ends in 2021. The 2021 value should not be compared directly with the 2024 values in other series.
Hotel occupancy is an index (percent, not a count), so a 2016-rebased index of occupancy represents percentage-point changes from baseline, not proportional recovery. The occupancy rate in 2024 (66.3%) exceeds the 2016 rate (56.7%) — a level recovery — but this reflects scarcity (fewer rooms) as much as demand strength.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Nominal vs. real series
No CPI deflation is applied in this analysis. The USVI CPI series is available only through 2021 and has a questionable 2018 value. No alternative USVI-specific deflator is available through 2024–2025.
The following series are already expressed in constant (real) dollars and are used as-is:

BEA Table 1.2: Real GDP (chained 2012 $)
BEA Table 2.3: Real value added by industry (chained 2012 $)

All other monetary series (USVIBER expenditures, Census receipts and payroll, World Bank receipts) are presented in nominal current USD. Comparisons across years should account for general inflation; this analysis does not attempt to adjust for it.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Limitations
Tourism ≠ GDP. BEA’s accommodation and food services value added excludes tourism-related retail, air transportation, recreation, and other sectors. It also includes consumption by residents. The sector’s GDP share understates the full economic footprint of tourism and overstates how much of the sector’s activity is visitor-driven.
Overnight tourists ≠ hotel guests. USVIBER’s “tourists” count includes villa rentals, short-term rentals, and other non-hotel accommodation. The overnight tourist recovery at 57% of 2016 may reflect both the reduced hotel room inventory and the divergent recovery of the vacation rental segment.
FRED L&H employment is not tourism employment. The L&H aggregate includes performing arts, museums, gambling (NAICS 71) alongside hotels and restaurants (NAICS 72). For USVI, this distinction is less critical because cultural attractions and casinos are a smaller share of the total than in mainland geographies. But the aggregate still overstates recovery in the hotel-and-restaurant segment relative to a tourism-specific series.
2017 is not a clean pre-hurricane baseline. The hurricanes struck in September. Full-year 2017 visitor counts (1.97M total; 535k overnight tourists) mix normal January–August activity with the September–December collapse. The 2016 value is used as the pre-hurricane baseline throughout.
Census 2022 was collected during COVID recovery. The 2022 Economic Census reference period (calendar year 2022) is a point in recovery, not a stable equilibrium. Employment (1,650 accommodation jobs) and receipts ($241M for NAICS 721) both reflect an industry still rebuilding from overlapping hurricane and pandemic shocks.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Software and reproducibility
All analysis was conducted in Python 3.14 using pandas 3.1, plotly 7.1, and associated packages listed in requirements.txt. The project is organized as a reproducible workflow:

Raw data in data/raw/ — never modified
Cleaning and validation in src/cleaning.py and src/validation.py
Cleaned intermediate datasets in data/interim/
Analysis notebooks in notebooks/
Publication via Quarto 1.10 in reports/

To reproduce: install dependencies from requirements.txt, run notebooks 01–06 in order, then run quarto render from the project root.

title: After the Storm
text:
In September 2017, Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck the U.S. Virgin Islands within two weeks of each other. The territory took a direct hit from two Category 5 storms, destroying hotel infrastructure, damaging or closing Virgin Islands National Park, and disrupting the economy that tourism had sustained for decades. Three years later, before recovery was complete, COVID-19 closed borders and halted cruise shipping.
This study draws on data spanning roughly 25 years across six primary sources to document how the USVI tourism economy has moved through those shocks — and what recovery looks like in 2024 and 2025. Source coverage varies: USVIBER provides selected years from 2000 and annual data from 2010; FRED employment begins in 1990; BEA data run 2002–2021/2022.
One headline stands out: total visitor arrivals have nearly returned to their 2016 level, but the composition has shifted fundamentally. Overnight visitors, who generate the large majority of tourism revenue, remain at roughly half their pre-hurricane baseline. Total air arrivals have recovered past their 2016 level, but that recovery is concentrated in same-day air excursionists — the overnight segment of air travel has not recovered in step.

title: After the Storm
text:
In September 2017, Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck the U.S. Virgin Islands within two weeks of each other. The territory took a direct hit from two Category 5 storms, destroying hotel infrastructure, damaging or closing Virgin Islands National Park, and disrupting the economy that tourism had sustained for decades. Three years later, before recovery was complete, COVID-19 closed borders and halted cruise shipping.
This study draws on data spanning roughly 25 years across six primary sources to document how the USVI tourism economy has moved through those shocks — and what recovery looks like in 2024 and 2025. Source coverage varies: USVIBER provides selected years from 2000 and annual data from 2010; FRED employment begins in 1990; BEA data run 2002–2021/2022.
One headline stands out: total visitor arrivals have nearly returned to their 2016 level, but the composition has shifted fundamentally. Overnight visitors, who generate the large majority of tourism revenue, remain at roughly half their pre-hurricane baseline. Total air arrivals have recovered past their 2016 level, but that recovery is concentrated in same-day air excursionists — the overnight segment of air travel has not recovered in step.

title: After the Storm
text:
The two shocks




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Total visitors include overnight tourists and same-day excursionists (cruise and air day-trip). The difference in shock depth between the two series is visible: the hurricane hit cruise and overnight visitors roughly equally; COVID virtually halted cruise while overnight visitors declined less sharply.




The 2017 hurricane shock cut total arrivals to 76% of their 2016 level within the same calendar year — notable given that the storms struck in September, meaning the first eight months of 2017 were largely normal. By 2018, the decline deepened as the full damage to hotel inventory became apparent.
COVID-19 in 2020 produced a collapse of different character: cruise shipping stopped almost entirely (cruise passengers fell to 25% of their 2019 level), while overnight tourists declined less sharply (to about 32% of 2019). The territory’s isolation and the absence of large-group gatherings may have made it modestly attractive to small-party leisure travelers once borders reopened.

title: After the Storm
section: A recovery that isn’t what it looks like
text:
A recovery that isn’t what it looks like




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Recovery index, 2016 = 100. Total arrivals near the baseline conceals the divergence between cruise recovery and the persistent deficit in overnight tourist visits.




As of 2024, the index looks deceptively healthy at the top line. Total arrivals sit at 97% of their 2016 baseline. But that recovery in total arrivals masks a stark difference in visitor value. USVIBER data for 2024 imply an average of approximately $2,350 per overnight tourist trip, compared with roughly $450 per cruise passenger stop and roughly $400 per air excursionist — both in nominal 2024 dollars. These are implied averages per arrival in their respective categories, not daily spending estimates.
Air visitor arrivals — tourists plus same-day air excursionists — actually reached 109% of their 2016 level by 2024. But this recovery is concentrated in air excursionists (day-trippers), which rose from about 140k in 2016 to 527k in 2024. Overnight tourists in 2024 stood at 57% of their 2016 level — barely higher than immediately after the hurricanes. Employment and accommodation capacity, measured in hotel rooms, tell a compatible story: the sector is operating at roughly 80–90% of its pre-storm scale, but on a visitor base that has not recovered.

title: After the Storm
text:
What the park shows
Virgin Islands National Park on St. John covers roughly 60 percent of the island’s land area. Its visitation has followed a markedly different trajectory than territory-wide overnight tourist arrivals, making the two series an interesting comparative indicator — though they measure different things and cannot be treated as equivalent.




                            
                                            


Figure 3: VIIS NP visitation vs. overnight tourists (both indexed to 2016 = 100). The park’s steep decline after 2017 reflects both the hurricane damage to trails and facilities and the collapse in overnight tourism. Its recovery to and past the 2016 level by 2024 is an unresolved divergence from the broader overnight tourist count.




VIIS NP visitation reached 103% of its 2016 level in 2024 and 115% in 2025. Overnight tourists, by USVIBER’s count, remained at 57% of 2016. The divergence is substantial enough to warrant investigation. Possible explanations include: changes in how NPS counts day-use visitors, increased use of the park by short-term rental guests (not counted as hotel tourists), or different recovery trajectories across segments of the overnight market. This is an open analytical question, not a resolved finding.

title: After the Storm
text:
Accommodation capacity




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Hotel room inventory and L&H employment indexed to 2016. Both declined sharply after the hurricanes — hotel rooms steeply in 2018 as damage became clear — and neither has fully recovered.




Hotel room inventory tracked by USVIBER’s annual survey stood at 82% of its 2016 level by 2024. The U.S. Census Economic Census (which counts only payroll-filing establishments) shows a more severe contraction: 2,039 rooms in 2022 versus a 2012 peak of 5,027 — a 59% decline. The Census and USVIBER series use different methodologies and should not be directly compared, but they agree on the direction: accommodation capacity has not recovered.
Leisure and Hospitality employment (FRED, seasonally adjusted) ran at 91% of its 2016 annual average in 2024 — closer to baseline than hotel rooms. This may reflect leaner staffing in surviving hotels, or expanded employment in the food and entertainment segment that comprises a large share of the L&H aggregate.
A note on hotel occupancy: USVIBER reports a 2024 occupancy rate of 66.3%, the highest in the available annual series since at least 2000. High occupancy on a reduced room base means the remaining hotels are operating at high utilization; it does not, by itself, establish their financial performance, since room rates, operating costs, and revenue data are not available. This pattern is consistent with either intensive use of surviving capacity, or with constrained supply relative to demand — or both.

title: After the Storm
text:
What the broader economy shows
Aggregate GDP and tourism activity tell different stories about the post-hurricane economy. BEA data show that USVI real GDP remained relatively stable in 2017 and grew in 2018–2021, even as visitor arrivals and accommodation revenue remained severely depressed. BEA attributed some of this growth to government spending and private fixed investment, which likely reflect hurricane response and reconstruction activity. These patterns illustrate how economic production can recover through activity outside the visitor economy while tourism itself remains impaired. This analysis does not estimate the contribution of federal disaster assistance to GDP.




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Accommodation and food services as a share of USVI nominal GDP, 2002–2021 (BEA data). The sector’s GDP share fell from roughly 13% in 2015 to 6% in 2020 before rebounding to 11% in 2021. Important caveat: Accommodation and food services value added is not equivalent to tourism GDP — it includes resident consumption and excludes tourism-related retail, transportation, and recreation.




Accommodation and food services value added — the broadest BEA measure of the sector’s economic contribution — fell from 13% of GDP in 2015 to 11.5% in 2017, collapsed to 6% in 2020, and rebounded to 11% in 2021, the last year BEA data are available. The rebound to 11% is encouraging but still below the pre-hurricane trend, and the GDP denominator during 2018–2021 likely reflects activity beyond the visitor economy. The sector had not returned to its pre-hurricane GDP share by 2021.

title: After the Storm
text:
Unresolved questions
This analysis surfaces several questions that the data alone cannot resolve:
Why have overnight tourists not recovered to 2016 levels? The hotel room deficit is real and constrains overnight capacity. Whether demand has also changed — in ways that would persist even if full capacity were restored — cannot be established from the available data. Possible factors worth investigating include the competitive position of other Caribbean destinations, traveler preference shifts following the pandemic, and long-term income effects from the post-hurricane period. These are open questions, not demonstrated findings.
Is the VIIS NP recovery real? The park exceeding its 2016 baseline while overnight tourists remain at 57% is a significant divergence. Either the park is drawing more visitors per overnight tourist (higher park utilization), or there is a visitor category being counted by NPS but not by USVIBER. This deserves direct investigation with NPS staff.
What does 66% occupancy on a smaller room base actually mean for the economy? High occupancy on reduced inventory may reflect healthy operating margins at surviving hotels while masking a smaller aggregate economic contribution. The Census 2022 data (1,650 accommodation employees vs. 3,876 in 2012) suggests the surviving hotel sector is operating at significantly reduced staffing levels.
The full exploratory analysis is in the Analysis companion. Data sources, variable definitions, and methodological choices are documented in the Data Dictionary and Methodology pages.

Important definitions: - NPS recreation visits ≠ territory-wide tourist arrivals - A person may visit multiple times; the park counts each visit separately - Park closures and access conditions affect counts (October–December 2017: near-zero counts due to hurricane damage and closure) - Cruise passengers rarely enter either park; visitation is dominated by independent overnight visitors
2026 exclusion: 2026 monthly VIIS data shows 100,000–170,000 visits per month (January–June), approximately three times the 2025 equivalent months. This anomaly has not been explained; 2026 data is excluded from all analysis.
Aggregation rule: Sum monthly observations for annual totals; do not use the annual-file total directly if computing from monthly data (sums match exactly for all available years).

Geographic filter: Filter to GEOTYPE = 2 (territory level) for all .dat files. Island- and town-level rows (GEOTYPE 3, 5) will otherwise inflate territory totals.
Employment reference date: March pay period of the census year.
Guestrooms (RMRTRAN): Reference date is December 31 of the census year.

2007 and 2012: use A10 industry-total row (PSCODE/NAPCS = industry total)
2017 and 2022: use NAPCS product code 7003825000 (“Room or unit accommodation for travelers”) — the NAPCS Total row RMRTRAN is inconsistent across vintages and should not be used for guestroom counts.

Critical note on 2017: The Economic Census guestroom reference date is December 31, 2017 — approximately three months after Hurricanes Irma and Maria (September 6 and 19). The 2017 guestroom count (2,624) reflects post-hurricane inventory, not the pre-hurricane baseline. It should be labeled accordingly and not used as a pre-storm benchmark.
Monetary units: All Census monetary variables (RCPTOT, PAYANN) are in thousands of dollars ($1,000). Divide by 1,000 for millions.
Suppression flags: Cells with flag D are withheld to avoid disclosing individual company data. S = withheld for reliability. Do not treat suppressed cells as zero.
